segments.text: Joins: putting the rows of several tables back together.
A well designed database splits its data. Students live in one table, courses in another.
Enrolment only stores the two ids, as foreign keys. To read who takes what, we follow those keys back.
That is what a join does: it pairs the rows whose keys match.
Start with an inner join of course and enrolment. The ON condition says how rows match: the course ids must be equal.
Databases matches three enrolments, Python two, and Statistics one. Each match becomes a row of the result.
Marketing finds no partner, so it disappears. An inner join keeps only the rows that match.
JOIN on its own means INNER JOIN.
What if we want every course, even the empty ones? Use a LEFT JOIN.
It keeps every row of the left table. Marketing comes back, and its enrolment columns are filled with NULL.
Now keep only the rows where the enrolment side is NULL. This is an anti-join: it finds the courses nobody takes.
Here, just Marketing.
A RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image: it keeps every row of the right table. Most people swap the tables and write LEFT.
A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps the unmatched rows of both sides. Statistics students on the left, Python students on the right: nobody takes both, so every row has a NULL.
A CROSS JOIN has no condition at all. It pairs every row with every row: three students times four courses gives twelve rows.
Forget the join condition, and this is what you get by accident.
A self-join joins a table with itself, under two aliases.
To find classmates, pair the enrolments of the same course. The condition a dot student id, less than b dot student id, stops a student pairing with themselves, and lists each pair once.
To sum up: inner keeps the matches. Left, right and full also keep the rows without a partner. Cross pairs everything, and a self-join compares a table with itself.
Practise it in the SQL section of the course site.
